opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the basic idea behind the time horizon work is that we wanted a single metric that tracks how capable AI agents are on real-world-ish tasks, in units that are intuitive. Instead of saying "this model gets 73% on some benchmark," we measure how long the tasks take skilled humans, and then find the task length at which the model succeeds about half the time. That gives you a number like "this model can do tasks that take an expert about an hour," and you can plot that over time. What we found is that it's been growing pretty steadily and exponentially, doubling roughly every seven months historically, and maybe faster more recently.

For AI R&D acceleration specifically, the appeal is that you can start to ask: what does the work of an AI researcher or research engineer actually consist of, and how long are the chunks of that work? A lot of research engineering is tasks on the order of hours, like implementing an experiment or debugging a training run. But the stuff that really drives progress often involves sustained, multi-day or multi-week projects with a lot of context, judgment calls, and recovering from dead ends. So if you have a trend line for time horizons, you can roughly extrapolate when models might reliably handle tasks on the scale of what researchers spend their days doing, and that gives you a forecast for when automation of meaningful chunks of AI research might start to substantially speed things up.

I want to be careful, though, because there are some big caveats. Our tasks are mostly software and ML engineering tasks that are relatively well-specified and automatically scorable, and real research is messier. Fifty-percent reliability is also very different from the reliability you'd need to hand off work without a human checking it. And there's a question of whether time horizon translates cleanly into speedup. A model that can do two-hour tasks doesn't necessarily make researchers twice as productive; that depends on how the work gets decomposed, how much oversight is needed, and where the bottlenecks are, like compute for experiments. So I think of time horizons as one useful input, a leading indicator that helps calibrate when we should be paying very close attention, rather than something that directly tells you "acceleration happens in year X." Pairing it with more direct measurements, like uplift studies with actual researchers, is important.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the basic idea behind the time horizons work is that there's this question that's really hard to answer directly, which is something like, "when will AI systems be doing a large fraction of the work of AI research?" And it's hard because AI research is this messy, heterogeneous thing. It's not one task. It's debugging, it's designing experiments, it's reading the literature, it's having taste about what's worth trying.

But one thing that seems pretty robustly true about human knowledge work, and about AI research in particular, is that a lot of it comes in chunks that take a certain amount of time. Some things take ten minutes. Some take a few hours. Some take a week or a month of sustained effort where you have to keep context and recover from mistakes and not go off the rails. And so the question "can a model do this task" ends up being pretty well predicted by "how long would it take a competent human to do this task."

So what we do is measure, for a given model, the length of task, in human time, at which it succeeds about half the time. And when you plot that against release date, you get this remarkably clean exponential, doubling roughly every seven months or so over the last several years, and arguably faster recently. I want to be careful about how much weight you put on the exact number, but the trend itself has been pretty stable.

The reason I think this is useful for the acceleration question specifically is that it gives you something concrete to extrapolate. If you think that automating most of AI research requires reliably doing things that take humans on the order of weeks or months, you can ask when the trend line gets there. And right now that points at something like a few years out, not decades. Which, if you believe it, matters a lot.

Now, I'd put a bunch of caveats on that. Our tasks are mostly self-contained software and research engineering tasks with clear success criteria. Real research is messier, it involves taste and coordination, and there's a gap between benchmark performance and actually being useful in a lab. We tried to get some sense of that gap with the uplift study we ran, where developers using AI tools were actually a bit slower, and that was a surprising result that I think should make people humble about reading too directly from benchmarks to real-world speedup. There's also the 50% versus 80% reliability question. The horizon at 80% is substantially shorter, and for a lot of real work you need high reliability.

But the thing I'd say in favor of the approach is that it's falsifiable. We're making a prediction, we can check it against new models as they come out, and so far it's held up. And having one interpretable number that you can argue about is a lot better than vibes. If the trend breaks, that tells us something important too.

astra-6.text:
I think time horizons give us a useful way of making that question more concrete. Rather than asking, “Is this model good at coding?” you can ask, “How long and complicated a task can it reliably complete on its own?” And then you can compare that to the tasks that actually make up AI research.

If a system can do things that take a researcher a few minutes, that can be useful, but the researcher still has to break the work down and supervise it pretty closely. As systems become able to handle tasks that would take a person hours or days, you can start delegating whole experiments or substantial pieces of implementation. That seems like a plausible point where you could get much more acceleration, because one person could oversee a lot more work.

But I wouldn't expect there to be a single time-horizon threshold that tells us when this happens. It matters whether the tasks we're measuring are representative of AI research. A model might be able to work through a long, well-specified engineering task while still being bad at choosing a promising research direction or interpreting an ambiguous result. Cost, reliability, and how much human attention the system needs also matter.

So I'd think of time horizons as one input into the prediction. You'd want to map out the work involved in AI progress, ask which parts systems can actually take over, and then look at what bottlenecks remain. Longer horizons are evidence that more substantial delegation is becoming possible; the acceleration depends on whether that delegation frees up the resources that are actually limiting progress.

sol-6.1.text:
I think time horizons give us one useful way of making that question more concrete. Rather than asking whether a model is good at coding, we can ask: how long a task can it complete autonomously, where we measure the length by how long it would take a human? And then we can compare that with the tasks involved in doing AI research.

If a system can do tasks that take a human a few minutes, it can be a useful assistant, but a human still has to break the research process into small pieces and check the results. As systems become able to handle tasks that take hours or days, you can potentially delegate whole experiments: implement an idea, run it, look at what happened, and debug it. That could let a researcher supervise much more work in parallel.

But I wouldn't expect there to be one time horizon where we can confidently say, ‘Okay, now AI progress accelerates.’ It matters whether the tasks we're measuring are representative of AI research. It also matters how reliable the systems are, how much supervision they need, and whether the remaining bottleneck is researcher time or something like compute.

So the thing I'd want to do is connect the horizon measurements to actual research workflows: what fraction of the work can you delegate, and how much does that reduce the time or cost of getting a useful research result? The horizon is an informative input to that, rather than a complete answer by itself.
